title: Small Multifamily Renovation Guide: Duplex to Fourplex
metaDescription: Renovating a duplex, triplex or fourplex: phasing occupied units, separate vs shared systems, fire separation and egress basics, metering, and permits.
h1: Renovating Small Multifamily: A Practical Guide for Duplexes, Triplexes and Fourplexes
dek: Small multifamily rehabs combine house-scale construction with building-scale problems: tenants living next to the work, shared systems that serve every unit, fire separation between dwellings, and metering that decides who pays for utilities. Plan phasing, systems and code issues together, and the building becomes easier to finance, insure and manage.
keyTakeaways: Phasing is the core decision: renovate vacant units first, move tenants within the building when possible, and keep occupied units livable and safe.
Decide early whether to separate or keep shared heating, water heating and electrical service, because it shapes scope, cost and who pays utilities.
Fire separation between units and safe exits from every unit are the code issues that most often change scope in older two- to four-unit buildings.
Confirm the legal unit count and zoning before buying or adding units; an informal conversion can block financing and insurance.
Standardize finishes across units so turns, repairs and future renovations work from the same materials.

sections.h2: What makes a two- to four-unit renovation different from a single-family rehab?
sections.body:
In most of the United States, buildings with one to four units are financed with residential loans and many are built and permitted under residential codes, while five or more units move into commercial lending and the commercial building code. That makes two- to four-unit buildings a bridge between house flipping and apartment investing, and the rehab reflects both.

The construction itself looks like a house rehab: kitchens, baths, flooring, paint, windows, roofs, systems. What changes is everything around it.

First, there are people. Many small multifamily purchases come with some units occupied, and tenant rights continue through the sale. Work has to be planned around who lives where, what notice is required, and how to keep occupied units safe and functional.

Second, there are shared systems. A single boiler may heat every unit. One water heater may serve two apartments. A single electrical service may feed a house panel and unit subpanels in ways that were added over decades. Decisions about these systems affect every unit at once.

Third, there are separation and exit requirements. Each dwelling unit needs protection from fire in neighboring units and a safe way out. In older buildings, especially conversions, those features may be missing or compromised.

Fourth, there is the question of legal status. Many small multifamily buildings, especially houses converted to multiple units, have a complicated permit history. The legal unit count affects zoning, lending, insurance and taxes.

The rest of this guide covers each of these in turn.

sections.h2: How do you phase a renovation with tenants in place?
sections.body:
Phasing is the order in which units and building systems are renovated, and it is the decision that most affects both tenant relations and schedule.

Start with what is vacant. Renovating vacant units first creates finished, rentable space and sometimes a place to relocate a tenant from a unit that needs heavier work. Where leases and local law allow, an in-building move to a newly renovated unit can be a good deal for everyone.

For occupied units, decide which work can be done with tenants present and which needs the unit vacant. Common categories:
- Exterior work, roof, windows done from outside, landscaping, common hallways and basements can usually proceed with tenants in place, with notice and attention to access and safety
- Systems work that interrupts heat, water or power needs advance notice and should be scheduled to minimize outages, often by staging new systems before switching over
- Kitchen and bath remodels inside an occupied unit are disruptive and may require temporary arrangements, or are better done at turnover

Respect notice and entry rules. State and local law sets how much notice landlords must give to enter units, and some cities have specific requirements for construction in occupied buildings, such as tenant protection plans. Know them before you schedule.

Keep occupied units safe. That means maintaining exits, keeping smoke and carbon monoxide alarms working, controlling dust, including lead-safe practices in pre-1978 buildings, and restoring essential services at the end of each workday.

Finally, communicate. A simple written schedule and a point of contact reduce complaints and help tenants plan around noise and outages.

sections.h2: Should heating, water and electrical systems be shared or separate?
sections.body:
Many small multifamily buildings were built with or evolved into shared systems. Whether to keep them shared or separate them is one of the biggest scope decisions in the rehab.

Heating. Older buildings often have a single boiler with radiators in every unit, or a single furnace feeding ducts that serve more than one apartment. A shared system means the owner pays for heat and controls the temperature, and that cost has to be built into rents. Separating heat, typically by installing a furnace or heat pump in each unit, shifts the cost to tenants and gives them control, but requires space, ductwork or equipment for each unit, and electrical or gas capacity to support it.

Water heating. A shared water heater simplifies equipment but means the owner pays for hot water and one failure affects every unit. Separate units add equipment and space but isolate problems.

Electrical. Each unit should have its own panel serving only that unit, with circuits clearly labeled. Older conversions sometimes have circuits that cross between units or common areas wired to a tenant's panel. Untangling that is often required by code during renovation and is necessary before separate metering works correctly.

The decision depends on the building and the market. In some markets tenants expect heat included and owner-paid heat is normal. In others, separate utilities are the norm and owner-paid systems put the building at a disadvantage. The physical constraints of the building, like basement space, chimney and venting options, and electrical service capacity, often settle the question.

Whatever you choose, size equipment to the actual load and document what serves what, so future repairs and turns are straightforward.

sections.h2: How does metering work, and when should you separate meters?
sections.body:
Metering determines who gets the utility bill. It is related to but separate from the question of shared equipment.

Electric. Most buildings have, or can be converted to, one electric meter per unit plus a house meter for common areas such as hall lighting, laundry and exterior lights. Separating meters usually involves the utility company, new meter sockets, new service equipment and permits. It also requires every unit's wiring to be truly separate, so no tenant pays for another unit or the common areas.

Gas. Where gas serves separate furnaces, water heaters or ranges in each unit, separate meters let tenants pay their own bills. Gas meter separation involves the gas utility and new piping, and the utility will have its own requirements for meter location and venting clearances.

Water. Water is often on a single meter per building, with the owner paying and recovering the cost through rent. Some jurisdictions allow submetering or ratio billing, where the owner bills tenants for water based on submeters or a formula. Rules on this vary widely by state and city, and some restrict or prohibit it, so check before you plan on it.

The value of separating meters is that utility costs shift to tenants, the owner's operating expense drops and conservation tends to improve when tenants pay their own usage. The cost is the conversion work and coordination with utilities, which can add steps to the schedule.

If you plan to separate meters, decide early. It affects electrical and plumbing scope, needs utility coordination that may take time, and is easiest to do when walls and service equipment are already being opened.

sections.h2: What should you know about fire separation and egress in older buildings?
sections.body:
Two life-safety concepts drive much of the code scope in small multifamily: separation between units and the ability to get out.

Fire separation means the walls and floor-ceiling assemblies between dwelling units are built to resist fire for a required period, and that openings and penetrations in those assemblies are protected. In a purpose-built older two-flat or fourplex, separation may have been adequate by the standards of its time but compromised since by holes for pipes, wires and ducts, by removed plaster, or by doors that no longer close and latch. In a single-family house that was later divided into units, separation may never have been built at all.

During a renovation, especially when walls and ceilings are opened, expect code officials to look at separation. Typical fixes include fire-rated drywall assemblies, sealing penetrations with fire-stopping materials, and providing appropriate doors between units and shared spaces. Exact requirements depend on the code adopted locally, the building's construction and whether a sprinkler system is present.

Egress means every unit has a safe path out, and sleeping rooms have an emergency escape opening, typically a window meeting size and sill-height requirements, unless the building is otherwise protected. Upper units in older buildings may rely on a single interior stair, a rear porch stair or an exterior fire escape. The condition of those stairs, porches and railings is a frequent issue, and in some cities rear porches are subject to specific inspection or rebuild requirements.

Alarms round it out: smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in each unit, often interconnected within the unit and sometimes required in common areas. Ask your contractor and the building department what the local code requires before finalizing scope.

sections.h2: How do you confirm the legal unit count before you buy?
sections.body:
A building advertised as a triplex may be legally a triplex, a legal duplex with an informal third unit, or a single-family house divided without permits. The difference affects value, financing, insurance and what you can do in the rehab.

Checks to run before purchase:
- Zoning. Confirm the property's zoning allows the number of units being used. Some areas allow multiple units by right; some allow existing nonconforming buildings to continue but not to expand; some have rules about what happens if a unit sits vacant for a long period.
- Permit and certificate records. Look for the original construction permit or certificate of occupancy showing unit count, and for permits on any conversions.
- Assessor and tax records. The property's classification there often reflects what the jurisdiction believes it is.
- Utility meters. The number of meters can suggest how the building was permitted, though informal conversions sometimes share meters.
- Physical clues. A basement or attic unit with low ceilings, inadequate egress windows or no separate heat is often an informal addition.

If a unit is not legal, the options are to legalize it through permits and code upgrades where zoning allows, to remove it and use the space differently, or to buy at a price that reflects the building's legal use. Do not plan on a lender, appraiser or insurer ignoring the issue.

Genstone's free Pre-Offer Rehab Review can help you price what a legalization scope might involve, such as egress, fire separation and systems separation, so the decision is made before closing rather than after.

sections.h2: What finishes and specifications work best for small multifamily?
sections.body:
Small multifamily units are rentals first, so finishes should be chosen for durability, ease of repair and consistency across units.

Flooring. Water-resistant hard flooring such as luxury vinyl plank holds up to turnover and pets, and individual planks can usually be replaced. On upper floors, think about sound. Hard flooring transmits footfall noise to the unit below more than carpet does, and some buildings or associations require underlayment with sound-reducing properties. Even where it is not required, a quality underlayment reduces complaints.

Paint. Pick one wall color and one trim color for all units, with a scrubbable finish. Touch-ups then blend and paint can be stocked.

Kitchens and baths. Use durable, widely available cabinets, solid-surface or quartz-type counters if the rent level supports them, or a quality laminate if not, and fixtures from a line that will remain available for replacement parts.

Laundry. Shared laundry in a basement, or hookups in each unit, affects rent, plumbing and electrical scope. In-unit hookups need drain, supply, venting and electrical capacity, and on upper floors a pan and drain under the washer reduces leak risk to the unit below.

Sound and privacy. When walls and ceilings between units are open for fire separation work, adding insulation for sound is inexpensive relative to the benefit in tenant satisfaction.

Exterior and common areas. Hallways, stairs, entries and exterior are the first impression for every prospective tenant. Lighting, durable flooring and secure entry hardware make a large difference to how the whole building rents.

Write these choices down as the building's standard, so future turns use the same products.

sections.h2: How should you budget and schedule a small multifamily rehab?
sections.body:
Budgeting for small multifamily combines per-unit costs with building-wide costs, and both need their own lines.

Per-unit items include each unit's kitchen, bath, flooring, paint, fixtures, appliances, and unit-level systems like a furnace or water heater if separate. These repeat, so pricing and quantities can be developed once and multiplied, with adjustments for each unit's condition.

Building-wide items include the roof, exterior envelope, foundation, common areas, shared mechanical systems, electrical service and meter work, sewer lateral, fire separation work, egress stairs and porches, site work and parking. These are often the largest and least predictable costs, and they are where contingency should be concentrated.

Schedule is shaped by phasing. Vacant units can move quickly. Occupied units depend on lease timing, notice requirements and tenant cooperation. Building-wide work may have to wait for weather, utility coordination or a period when the systems can be shut down.

A useful approach is to separate the rehab into stages:
- Stage one: building-wide safety and envelope items, such as roof, egress, fire separation repairs and any urgent systems issues
- Stage two: vacant unit renovations, using a standard spec
- Stage three: occupied units at turnover or with relocation
- Stage four: common areas and exterior finish, when heavy work is done

If the rehab is financed, coordinate the draw schedule with these stages so funds release as each completed stage is verified. That keeps lender inspections simple and ties payment to finished work.

faqs.q: Can I renovate a duplex with tenants living in one unit?
faqs.a: Usually yes, with planning. Work in the vacant unit can proceed while you control dust, noise and shared-system shutdowns that affect the occupied side. Give the notice required by state and local law for any entry or service interruption, keep exits and alarms working, and use lead-safe practices if the building is pre-1978. Larger work inside the occupied unit is often best done at turnover or with a temporary relocation where leases and local rules allow.

faqs.q: Do I have to separate utilities when I renovate a small multifamily building?
faqs.a: Not always. Many jurisdictions allow shared heat or water with the owner paying, recovered through rent. Code may still require each unit to have its own electrical panel serving only that unit, and separation becomes necessary if you plan to meter units separately. Whether separating is worthwhile depends on local tenant expectations, the building's physical constraints and the cost of conversion compared to the operating savings over your hold.

faqs.q: What is the most common code issue in older small multifamily buildings?
faqs.a: Fire separation and egress come up most often. Older buildings and conversions frequently have gaps in the fire-resistant construction between units, penetrations that were never sealed, and doors that do not close and latch. Upper units may depend on deteriorated rear stairs or porches. Bedrooms may lack proper emergency escape windows. These issues often surface once walls are opened, so price for them in buildings where the history is uncertain.

faqs.q: Is a fourplex financed differently from a five-unit building?
faqs.a: Typically yes. In most cases, properties with one to four units can use residential financing, including conventional, FHA and many investor loans such as DSCR loans, while five or more units generally require commercial multifamily financing with different underwriting. That is one reason two- to four-unit buildings are popular with smaller investors. The legal unit count matters here, since a lender will underwrite based on the units the property is legally permitted to have.
